analysis.one_liner: Caps interest rates on consumer credit at 15%, including all finance charges and fees.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap consumer interest at 15% was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in March 2009 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to cap the annual percentage rate on any consumer loan at 15% on unpaid balances, counting every finance charge, and it bars lenders from stacking fees to get around the cap [S3]. The Federal Reserve could temporarily raise the ceiling for up to 18 months if market rates rise and lender safety is threatened, and credit unions are exempt [S3]. A lender who charges more would forfeit the interest on the loan, and a borrower could sue to recover everything paid above the cap within two years [S3]. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never taken up [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households carrying revolving credit card debt or taking out high-rate consumer loans. Credit card rates commonly run well above 15%, and a cap that counts all finance charges and fees would directly lower what those borrowers pay, with a two-year window to recover unlawful charges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households carrying high-interest credit card debt

how_it_helps.text: Caps the APR on any extension of consumer credit at 15% on unpaid balances, inclusive of all finance charges, so lenders cannot exceed it through interest or charges rolled into the rate.
Bars fee evasion: fees that are not technically finance charges cannot be used to get around the cap, and their total cannot exceed the total finance charges on the loan.
Lets a borrower recover, within two years, the entire amount of interest, finance charges, or fees paid above the legal rate, and makes a knowing violation forfeit the loan's interest.
Builds in a safety valve: the Federal Reserve may raise the ceiling above 15% for periods of up to 18 months if market rates rise and lender safety and soundness are threatened.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, subprime and high-rate installment lenders, and other consumer lenders whose business models depend on rates above 15%. Indirectly, borrowers with poor credit could lose access to legal credit, because lenders who price risk above the cap would likely stop lending to them rather than lend at a loss.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers and high-rate lenders

drawbacks.text: The cap applies to every extension of consumer credit, so lenders who set rates based on a borrower's risk could simply stop lending to riskier borrowers; those consumers could lose access to credit cards and installment loans entirely rather than get them at 15%.

The bill gives the Federal Reserve discretion to lift the ceiling for up to 18 months when lender safety is threatened, which means the 15% cap could be suspended repeatedly during periods of rising rates.

Because the cap would apply to rates charged by banks and nonbank lenders alike, an abrupt transition could tighten credit availability for households at a time when, in 2009, the economy was already in a deep recession and lenders were pulling back.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of households paying credit card rates in the 20-30% range, a hard 15% cap counting all fees would be a direct, meaningful cost cut, and the fee-evasion ban and refund right make it harder to dodge than a nominal cap. The serious cost is on the other side of the credit market: risk-based pricing exists because some borrowers are much more likely to default, and a uniform 15% cap would likely price those borrowers out of legal credit altogether. The bill's drafters partially addressed this with the Fed's temporary escape valve and the credit union exemption, but the access problem for high-risk borrowers is real and the bill does not solve it.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee never took the bill up after it was referred there, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Maurice Hinchey and six original cosponsors introduced the bill on March 19, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
Eighteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total.
No further action was ever taken: no committee markup, no floor vote, nothing after the referral, and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and other lenders charging rates above 15% kept their existing pricing power, and borrowers gained nothing.

for.name: Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Interest Rate Reduction Act and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 18 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other action on it was recorded.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill saw no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors were House Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no record of opposition or a partisan split exists.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer banks
industries.note: Card APRs commonly run above 15%, and the cap counts all finance charges and fees, so issuers would lose a large share of the interest revenue they collect from revolving borrowers — the same charges the bill would refund to consumers.
These lenders charge rates far above 15%; a national cap that applies to any extension of consumer credit would end their core product unless the Fed lifted the ceiling.
The bill expressly exempts insured credit unions from the cap, giving them a competitive advantage over banks and card issuers while their members keep access to their loans.
